e.t: This word is a proper name, preserved as “Abelbaithamaacha” or “Avelvethamaakha.” It identifies a specific named place or person rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Kings 15:29. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, its precise referent cannot be explained further without adding information beyond the name itself.

This verb means “ignorant” or “ignore”: it can describe lacking knowledge or failing to recognize something. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used for not knowing, overlooking, or acting without awareness, depending on the sentence. It occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, including passages from Genesis, Leviticus, Numbers, Samuel, Daniel, and other books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek verb means “compress; press tight”: it describes squeezing or forcing something into a tighter condition. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times—once in Psalms and three times in 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being pressed and the surrounding sentence.

Aithan, also rendered Ethan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies particular people named Aithan or Ethan. The name occurs seven times across seven verses, chiefly in 1 Chronicles and once in Psalms. Its precise reference depends on the person named in each passage, but its basic function remains that of a proper name.

This is a proper name rendered as “Ainōn; Enon.” It functions as a name rather than as a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Joshua 15:61 and once in Psalms 17:4. Without the surrounding verse text, its specific referent cannot be described further here, but the word itself identifies a named entity in those passages. “Ainōn” and “Enon” are the two supplied renderings of the same name.

This verb means “ask”: to request something from another person. It describes the act of making a request, whether directed toward a human being or toward God, while the surrounding passage determines what is being requested. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 77 times, showing a broad and ordinary use for requesting or seeking something. Its basic sense remains the same across these uses: someone asks for something from someone else.

This word refers to an “alabaster box,” a container made from alabaster. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 21:13. The word itself identifies the kind of container; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain how that object functions in that particular setting. Its basic meaning remains the same: an alabaster vessel or box used to hold something.

gl: at another time; at other times
d: at another time; at other times

e.h: At Another Time or At Other Times
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic senses are “at another time” and “at other times”. It points to a different time rather than the present time being discussed, and it can refer either to one other occasion or to other occasions more generally. In the Greek LXX, it appears once, in 2 Maccabees 13:10. The surrounding sentence is needed to determine whether it points to one earlier or later occasion in that passage.

Amasia is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:34. Because the available information gives the name and reference but not the verse text, it does not establish additional details about Amasia’s family, actions, position, or significance. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal name “Amasia,” rather than a common word describing an object, action, quality, or relationship.

This proper noun refers to an Ammonite, identifying a person connected with Ammon in the Greek Old Testament. It is a name or designation rather than a general action, quality, or object. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 1 Samuel 11. Its exact role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic reference remains an Ammonite person.

This Greek LXX noun means “fisherman” or “angler,” referring to a person who catches fish. It is a straightforward name for someone engaged in fishing rather than a description of an emotion, action, or spiritual quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Isaiah 19:8. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a fisherman or angler.

This Greek verb means “eliminate” or “take up.” It can describe removing a person or thing, bringing something away, or taking it up, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 73 times, so its central idea is established across many passages rather than being limited to one event. The surrounding words determine whether the action emphasizes removal, destruction, or taking something away. It is a verb describing an action, not a person, object, or quality.

This verb means “return safely” or “recover.” It describes coming back from danger, difficulty, or loss in a restored condition. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 26 times, so its central idea is broader than one particular situation: a person or thing is brought back safely or restored. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on safe return or recovery.

This verb means “reflected” or “echoed,” describing something repeated or sent back rather than produced as a wholly new sound or image. It can refer to an effect that answers or reproduces what came before. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:18. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of what is being reflected or echoed.

This Greek LXX verb means “do in return”: it describes responding to someone by carrying out a corresponding action. Its basic sense is reciprocal, focusing on what one person does back in response to another person’s action. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Leviticus and once in 1 Maccabees. The surrounding verse determines the specific action being returned.

This Greek LXX verb means “renounce”: to openly refuse or give up a person, claim, obligation, or course of action. It describes a deliberate act of disowning or rejecting rather than a passing feeling or accidental loss. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, including books such as 1 Kings, Job, Zechariah, Wisdom, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what the surrounding passage says is being renounced.

Asebi is a proper name, with “Asevi” given as another form of the same name. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 6:30. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, the name’s specific family or narrative role cannot be explained from this word alone. Its basic meaning is the personal designation Asebi/Asevi.

Ausitis is a proper name, also given as “Afsitis.” It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament wording of Job, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs three times in the Greek LXX text, all within Job: at Job 1:1, 32:2, and 42:17. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent in each occurrence cannot be stated more specifically, but its basic function is to name Ausitis.

Achaz, also rendered Akhaz, is a proper name identifying a named figure in the Old Testament Greek translation. It is not a descriptive word or action; its function is to designate this person by name. The name occurs 38 times across 37 Old Testament verses in the LXX, beginning at 2 Kings 15:38 and continuing through Micah 1:1. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This adjective means “inanimate,” describing something without life. It identifies an object or thing as lifeless rather than living, and its exact force in a sentence depends on what object or comparison is being discussed. In the Greek Septuagint corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in the Wisdom of Solomon: once in Wisdom 13:17 and once in Wisdom 14:29. These references show that the word is used as a descriptive term for a lifeless thing, not as a personal name or action.

Baithsaan, also rendered Vethsaan, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named place or entity rather than describing an action, quality, or relationship. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Chronicles 7:29. Since the verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage must be understood from its surrounding context.

This word is a proper name, identified as “Beēr; Vir.” It refers to a specific named person, place, or other individual in the passage, rather than expressing a general action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Genesis 26:34. The available information identifies the name but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the particular referent or role there.

This Greek LXX noun means “nursing at the breast,” referring to the act or condition of feeding an infant from the breast. It names a stage of bodily care associated with a nursing mother, rather than a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 16:7. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains nursing at the breast.

Gedeōn is a proper name, referring to the man known as Gedeon, also rendered Yetheon. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears 45 times across 43 verses, all in Judges, from Judges 6:11 through Judges 8:35. It identifies the same person throughout those passages rather than describing a quality, action, or general idea. The exact significance of the name in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic function is personal identification.

This word describes a discharge or a person suffering from gonorrhoea. It is an adjective, so it identifies a condition rather than naming an action. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs 14 times in 13 Old Testament verses, most often in Leviticus 15. It also appears in Numbers and 2 Samuel. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This verb means to distribute or spread something, describing the act of dividing it among people or extending it across an area. It presents distribution as an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 29:25. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly what is being distributed or spread there, but the basic meaning remains the intentional sharing or extension of something.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a fall or an error—an instance of going wrong or coming down from a proper position. Its basic meaning is brief and concrete rather than a broad description of a person’s character or an entire situation. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Jeremiah 19, so its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. The English rendering provided is “fall.”

This Greek LXX noun means “crossroad,” referring to a place where routes meet or pass through. It is used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings as a geographical term, especially in descriptions of boundaries and locations. The word occurs 27 times in the LXX corpus, with many occurrences in Joshua, Numbers, and Psalms. Its precise sense in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a meeting or passing point for routes.

This conjunction means “therefore.” It links a preceding reason or fact with a resulting conclusion, showing that what follows is presented as a consequence of what came before. In the LXX corpus, it appears 22 times, serving this connecting function in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its role is not to name an object or action, but to mark the logical step from an earlier statement to its outcome or conclusion.

This word means “dew,” the light moisture that settles on the ground, plants, or other surfaces, usually during the night. It is a noun naming this natural covering or deposit. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs 38 times, including passages describing dew upon the land, dew associated with blessing, and dew as an image in poetic language. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This verb means to laugh out or laugh loudly. It describes an audible, outward expression of laughter rather than a quiet inward feeling. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, including passages in Nehemiah, Psalms, and Wisdom. Its use can describe people laughing, and it can also portray laughter as an expressed response. The precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

This noun refers to “shaking out” or “violent shaking.” It describes a forceful movement in which something is shaken vigorously, rather than a gentle tremor. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Nahum 2:11, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains a powerful shaking or jostling action. It is a concrete noun naming the act or result of such violent movement.

This verb means “gather in the vintage,” referring to collecting grapes from the vine during harvest. It describes the act of gathering the produce of the vineyard rather than planting, tending, or storing it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Leviticus 25:5. Its precise force in that verse is shaped by the surrounding law about what may or may not be harvested.

This word is a proper name, referring to a person named Elead, also rendered Eleath. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:21. Because it is a personal name rather than a common noun or descriptive word, its basic function is to identify an individual, not to express an action, quality, or spiritual concept. The available information does not provide a separate meaning for the name itself.

Enōch, or Enokh, is a proper name used for people named Enoch in the Greek Old Testament and related writings. It does not function as a descriptive word with a separate ordinary meaning; it identifies a person by name. This name occurs 19 times in the Greek LXX corpus, across 17 verses, with most occurrences in the Old Testament portion and several in Genesis. Because more than one person bears this name, the surrounding passage is needed to identify which Enoch is meant in a particular verse.

“Mercifully” means in a merciful way—showing or extending compassion rather than acting harshly. As an adverb, it describes how an action is carried out, so it modifies a verb or statement rather than naming a person, thing, or quality by itself. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice, in 1 Samuel 12:22 and 2 Kings 6:3. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains merciful action.

This Greek LXX verb means to “rejoice over” or “exult over” someone or something. It describes an expression of gladness directed toward a particular object, rather than merely feeling happy in general. The word occurs 18 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so it is used across multiple biblical settings. Its precise force in any passage depends on what the rejoicing is directed toward and the surrounding verse. This LXX word remains distinct from Greek New Testament vocabulary.

This Greek LXX adjective means “easier,” describing something that requires less effort or is less difficult than another option. It is a comparative word, so it normally points to a more manageable course, task, or situation rather than simply saying that something is easy. The word occurs twice in the deuterocanonical Greek corpus, appearing once in Sirach and once in 1 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence and comparison.

This Greek LXX verb means “draw on; drag”: to pull something along or cause it to be brought forward. It describes an action of exerting force so that a person or thing moves in the direction of the one pulling. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise emphasis—whether pulling something physically or drawing it onward—depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains movement produced by pulling.

Zemmath is a proper name, referring to a person named Zemmath in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but as an individual name. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Chronicles 29:12. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the person’s specific role cannot be explained from the name alone.

This adjective means “our own,” marking something as belonging to or associated with the speaker and those joined with the speaker. It emphasizes a particular group’s possession or identity rather than someone else’s. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 21 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is used for this ordinary possessive idea in a range of passages. Its exact force in any verse depends on what group the surrounding sentence identifies as “our.”

This word is a proper name, given as “Thaimanōn; Themanon.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs five times, appearing once in Genesis, once in 1 Chronicles, and three times in Job. The available information identifies its naming function but does not state the person or place to which each occurrence refers.

Thēria (also rendered Thiria) is a proper name in the Greek LXX. The available lexical information identifies it by these name forms but does not specify whether it names a person, place, or something else, so its particular referent must be determined from the verse context. It occurs 62 times in the LXX corpus, from Genesis through the Epistle of Jeremiah.

Iekman is a proper name, rendered “Iekman,” rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 19:11. Because the available text does not include the surrounding verse, this cache identifies the name and its normal lexical function but does not determine whether the named referent is a person, place, or other specific entity. Its precise significance in Joshua 19:11 must therefore be read from that verse and its surrounding passage.

“Judaic” describes something connected with the Jewish people, their identity, or their religious life. As an adjective, it qualifies a person, practice, object, or matter as belonging to or associated with Judaism. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, this word occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 13:21. Since the surrounding verse text is not available here, the precise thing it describes in that occurrence cannot be stated, but its basic sense remains “Judaic”: relating to the Jewish community or its religious identity.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Iōnadab” or “Ionathav.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 16 times across 14 verses, including passages in 2 Samuel, 2 Kings, Psalms, and Jeremiah. Because it is a name, its basic meaning is the individual it identifies; the surrounding verse is needed to distinguish which person bearing the name is intended. The name appears in Old Testament narrative and related historical material, but the available information does not provide a further lexical definition.

This word means “cleansing”: the act or process of making something clean. As a noun, it can describe cleansing required in worship or cleansing associated with removing defilement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in four verses: twice in Leviticus and once each in Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Its basic meaning remains focused on becoming clean rather than describing a person, object, or action by itself. The surrounding passage determines what is being cleansed and why.

This conjunction means “and actually,” adding a confirming or emphatic point to what has just been said. It joins thoughts while drawing attention to the fact that the next statement is especially true, noteworthy, or contrary to what might have been expected. Its precise force depends on the sentence around it, but its basic function is to connect and reinforce an idea rather than introduce a separate subject. It appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus, all in 4 Maccabees.

This word means “burnt offering,” referring to an offering presented to God and burned in worship. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, especially in passages describing Israel’s sacrificial worship. The word occurs 57 times in the Greek Old Testament, with many occurrences in Leviticus and Numbers. Its meaning remains focused on the offering itself rather than on a general gift or sacrifice of any kind.

This Greek LXX noun means “bandage” or “wrapping,” referring to material used to bind or cover something. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 7:16. The word itself identifies a physical covering or binding, while the surrounding verse determines exactly how that image functions there. Its meaning is concrete and practical rather than a general description of healing, protection, or spiritual care.

Kendebaios, also rendered Kentheveos, is a proper name identifying a person rather than a general idea or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs five times, all in 1 Maccabees, from 1 Maccabees 15:38 through 16:8. The name itself does not describe an action, virtue, emotion, or spiritual concept; its function is to identify the same named individual wherever it appears. The person’s particular role in any passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative.

This noun refers to an omen or to divination—the practice of seeking meaning or guidance through signs. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it appears once, in Isaiah 2:6. Its meaning is therefore focused and specific rather than a broad term for every kind of prediction or religious practice. The exact force of the word in Isaiah depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which should be read alongside this basic sense.

This word means “raven,” the name of a black bird. It is a noun referring to the bird itself, whether mentioned in an animal list, a narrative, or a poetic question about God’s care for creatures. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times in 11 verses, from Genesis through Song of Songs. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it appears; the surrounding passage determines the particular point being made about the raven.

This Greek LXX verb means “strengthen”: to make someone or something stronger or more firmly established. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Wisdom 14:16. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the particular object or situation being strengthened cannot be stated safely. Its central idea remains the giving or receiving of greater strength, stability, or firmness, according to the sentence in which it appears.

Manthanain is a proper name, used to identify a particular place or named location rather than to express an action, quality, or general idea. It appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Numbers 21:18–19. The English rendering preserves the name as “Manthanain,” while the lexical record also gives the form “Manthanen.” Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further information about the place or its significance.

Marioth is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Nehemiah. The name is rendered “Marioth,” and the available lexical definition identifies it simply as “Mariōth; Marioth.” Its exact reference is determined by the person named in each passage, but the word itself functions as a proper name.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “to scourge” or “to whip”—to strike someone with a whip as punishment or severe beating. It describes an action rather than the whip itself, and its sense can be understood plainly wherever the surrounding passage mentions beating or scourging. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek Old Testament, including the books of Exodus, Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on that passage’s context.

Mesollam is a proper name identifying a person rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX, it appears twice, both times in 2 Kings: once at 2 Kings 21:19 and once at 2 Kings 22:3. The available wording preserves the name as “Mesollam,” so no broader meaning or translation sense is established here. Its significance in either passage must be understood from the surrounding verse and narrative context.

This word means “hire”: to engage someone for work or service. It is a verb, so it describes the act of bringing someone into service rather than naming the worker or the payment itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 15 times, appearing in passages from Genesis through 1 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on arranging for someone to serve or work. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Moocha or Mookha is a proper name, functioning as the designation of an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 19:6. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the individual’s role or significance in that passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as a personal name whose particular reference comes from its biblical context.

This word means “Nazarite,” referring to a person “consecrated by Nazarite vows.” It is a noun for someone identified by that consecration. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Judges 13:5. The term therefore points to a vow-defined status, not merely to a personal feeling or general devotion. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

Nephthaleim is a proper name, also rendered Nefthalim. It identifies a named figure or people in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears 52 times across 48 verses in the Greek Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel. Its precise reference in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a name throughout its use.

This Greek LXX adjective means “swimming,” describing something associated with swimming or movement through water. It is a descriptive word, not a name for a person, place, or event. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Wisdom 19:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense remains connected with swimming and water. [p03:word:lxx:L709293:identity, p03:word:lxx:L709293:occurrences, p01:word:lxx:L709293:reference:0]

Oba, also rendered Ova, is a proper personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:34. The name itself identifies a person in the biblical record; its precise significance beyond that name cannot be determined from the available lexical information. The spelling Oba or Ova reflects the two supplied forms of this name, not separate concepts.

“Likening” means making a comparison by showing that one thing resembles another. As a noun, this word points to the correspondence or resemblance itself rather than describing an action in progress. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, all in seven verses. Its uses range across Genesis, Psalms, Ezekiel, and Daniel, so the basic idea applies wherever something is presented as resembling, being compared with, or corresponding to something else. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being likened.

Ool is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX), referring to a person named Ool rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in this LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 3:20, and the available rendering preserves the name as “Ool.” Because no verse text or wider passage is included here, the name’s particular family or narrative setting must be understood from that passage, but the lexical meaning supplied is simply the personal name Ool.

This word means “when”. It is an adverb that points to the time at which something happens, happened, or is expected to happen. It commonly introduces or connects a time setting, helping the reader understand the order or occasion of an event. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 114 times, showing that it is a regular way to identify timing in biblical sentences. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

This noun refers to experience or emotional feeling—the inner response or passion a person undergoes. It can describe what someone feels or passes through, especially when emotion is being considered as a human experience. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 65 times, with most occurrences in 4 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word refers to the coast or to a place by the sea. As a noun, it can name a coastal area; as an adverb, it can describe location in relation to the sea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Deuteronomy, Judges, Isaiah, and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains a seaside or coastal location.

gl: point out at the same time
d: point out at the same time

e.h: A Word for Point Out At The Same
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “point out at the same time”. It describes an action in which something is indicated or brought forward concurrently with something else. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Maccabees 15:10. Because it occurs only there and no verse text is available here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains the simultaneous act of pointing something out.

This Greek LXX verb means “pat; impact.” It describes an action that makes contact with something or someone, whether by a light pat or a forceful impact. The word functions as an action word rather than a name or description. It occurs 395 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and action being described.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a person who is fettered—a prisoner held in bonds. It describes someone constrained or detained rather than free to go. The word occurs once in the Greek text represented here, at Wisdom 17:2, so its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context. Its central meaning remains clear: a captive person bound or confined. [p03:word:lxx:L710211:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L710211:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L710211:reference:0]

This verb means to wall all round—to surround a place with a protective or enclosing wall. It describes the act of enclosing something completely, rather than merely building one section of a wall. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs twice: once in Hosea and once in 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains clear: creating a complete barrier or enclosure around something.

This noun means “harm; malignancy,” referring to a damaging or harmful condition, quality, or action. It describes what brings injury or trouble rather than something beneficial or sound. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 69 times, showing a broad use for harm or malignancy across different settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains something harmful, damaging, or morally bad in effect.

This word means “age.” It is a noun referring to age as a stage or condition of life. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, so it is a recurring term rather than a rare expression. Its precise sense in a particular passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains age or the condition associated with being advanced in life.

This verb means “give besides”: to provide something in addition to what has already been given. It describes an added gift, payment, or provision rather than the first act of giving. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, in Genesis and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being given and what has already been provided, but its central idea is additional giving or supplying something extra.

This Greek LXX verb means “shut”: it describes closing something so it is no longer open or accessible. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Genesis 19:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of shutting or closing.

This word means “red.” It can describe something by its reddish color or function as a noun referring to a red one. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Genesis and twice in 1 Samuel. Its use is therefore specific and color-focused rather than a broad term for appearance. The word appears in passages associated with Genesis 25:25, 1 Samuel 16:12, and 1 Samuel 17:42, though the surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular force in each passage.

Rhamnon is a proper name preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Judges 10:5, and its English rendering is “Rhamnon.” The available information identifies the name but does not provide enough verse text or contextual detail to say whether it refers to a person, place, or something else. Its precise referent must therefore be determined from the surrounding passage.

Raphes, also written Rhafes, is a proper name referring to a specific person or place named in the Greek Old Testament. The name itself does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual idea; it identifies someone or something by name. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in 2 Kings 19:12 and once in Isaiah 37:12. Those passages are parallel accounts, but the surrounding verse text is needed to identify precisely what Raphes refers to in each occurrence.

This Greek LXX noun means “pen; fold,” referring to an enclosed space used to contain or gather something, especially animals. The central idea is a bounded enclosure rather than an open area. This Greek LXX noun refers to a cucumber or gourd, a type of produce. It names a food item rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 11:5. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is the name of this cultivated plant or its fruit.

This word means “wheat,” the grain crop used as food. It is a noun naming wheat itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 78 times, showing that it is a regularly used term for this important kind of grain. Its appearances range from Genesis through Song of Songs, within both historical and poetic books. Sousakim, also written Susakim, is a proper name used in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named figure rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. This noun means “tenth of a mile,” a unit used to describe distance. It refers to a measured length rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including passages in Daniel, 2 Maccabees, and Susanna. Because the word expresses a specific distance, its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding measurements and events described there.

This noun means “mixing together” or “commixture,” referring to the combining of separate things into one mixture. It is a term for the result or process of things being blended together, rather than for one individual object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 22:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a combination formed by mixing things together.

This noun means a “juncture” or “seam”—the place where separate parts meet or are joined together. It can describe a joining point, connection, or line of union rather than one of the parts by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Isaiah 41:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic picture is something joined at a meeting point. It is therefore a concrete term for the connection or seam formed where parts come together.

This noun means a companion at table—someone sharing a meal with another person. It refers to a fellow diner or meal companion, rather than describing the food or the act of eating itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 9:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary meaning is a person who sits and eats as another’s companion.

It can therefore refer to men acting or appearing as a group rather than as isolated individuals. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, across Numbers, Samuel, Kings, and Ezra, showing use for gathered human groups. Its central picture is of separate parts drawn together into one connected body or assembly.

Sōchōn is a proper name, rendered “Sokhon” in English. It identifies a person named in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. This adjective describes someone as miserable or suffering—living in a painful, distressed, or pitiable condition. It is a description of a person’s state rather than an action or command. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific situation, but the word itself points plainly to misery and suffering.

e.h: A Word for Three Times Over
e.t: This word is a verb that expresses an action or state. Its basic sense is “three times over”. It describes something occurring or being understood in a threefold measure. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Sirach 43:4. Because the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the surrounding passage. Still, the central idea remains clear: the word marks repetition or degree as threefold, emphasizing that something is done or present three times over.

This verb means to promise—to give someone a stated assurance that something will be done or given. It describes the act of making a commitment, rather than merely expressing a wish or possibility. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it appears four times, all in the deuterocanonical books Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on who is making the promise and what is promised, but its central meaning remains the deliberate giving of an assurance.

This verb means “fold over” or “drape over.” It describes placing one thing over another so that it bends, hangs, or covers it. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both within Exodus 26:12, so its available usage is concentrated in one passage rather than spread widely across the biblical text. As a verb, it expresses an action involving material or an object; the surrounding verse determines exactly what is folded or draped and how the action functions there.

This Greek LXX verb means “seize underneath,” describing an action in which something is taken from beneath or by reaching underneath it. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in Job, Ecclesiastes, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX word means “friend”—someone regarded with personal affection, loyalty, or closeness. It can describe a person as a friend or function as a noun for such a companion. The word appears 135 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this LXX corpus, showing that friendship is a recurring relational idea. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense remains a trusted or valued companion.

This noun refers to a blister or pustule, a raised skin lesion. It names a visible bodily condition rather than an action, person, or character trait. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Exodus 9:9–10, and its meaning remains centered on this physical ailment. This Greek LXX noun means “litter,” a conveyance used to carry a person. It names the object itself rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the LXX corpus, appearing in 2 Maccabees and Song of Songs. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains a litter: a carried seat or vehicle for transporting someone.

This adverb means “in a worse way,” describing how an action or situation happens when it is more seriously or badly than another. It focuses on the manner of an action rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 7:39. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense is a comparison pointing to a more negative manner or condition.

This adjective means “of gold” or “golden,” describing something made from gold or having its characteristic appearance. In the Greek Old Testament, it commonly describes objects, furnishings, ornaments, and other items associated with gold. The word occurs 200 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented in this corpus, so it is a well-established descriptive term rather than a rare expression. Its exact force—whether material, color, or appearance—depends on the noun and surrounding sentence.
